label: LS-split
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{LS-split}
Let $G$ be a split connected reductive $K$-group for $K/\mathbb{Q}_p$ a finite extension, $h$ its Coxeter number, and $I\subseteq G(K)$ a pro-$p$ Iwahori subgroup.  If $p-1>eh$, then there exists a saturated $p$-valuation $\omega$ on $I$.
head: environment
name: Lahiri-Sorensen

label: intro-existence
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{intro-existence}
Let $G$ be a connected reductive $K$-group, and assume that $T$ is weakly induced.  Then for any $x\in \mathcal B( G)$, $\omega_x$ is a saturated $p$-valuation on $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$.
head: environment

label: intro-polytope
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{intro-polytope}
If $G$ is quasisplit, $T$ is weakly induced, and $T(K)_{0+}=T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$, then there is an open convex polytope $U$ of the dominant base chamber $C\subseteq \mathcal A(S)$ given by
$$U=\left\{x\in \mathcal A(S)\,\Bigg|\, x=x_0+v, \quad \frac1{p-1}<\langle \alpha, v\rangle<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right)\quad \forall \alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}\right\}$$
such that $G_{x,0+}=G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ for each point $x\in U$. In other words, we get a distinct saturated $p$-valuation $\omega_x$ on $I$ for each $x\in U$, which is described by the Moy-Prasad filtration at the point $x$.  This subset $U$ is nonempty precisely when 
$$p-1>(m_\alpha \mathrm{ht}(\alpha)+1)\cdot e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Suppose that $G$ is a connected quasisplit semisimple $K$-group, and assume that 
$$p-1>\big(m_\alpha\mathrm{ht}(\alpha)+1\big)\cdot e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$.  Then there is an open convex nonempty polytope $U$ of $C\subseteq \mathcal A(S)$ given by 
$$U=\left\{x\in \mathcal A(S)\,\Bigg|\, x=x_0+v, \quad \frac1{p-1}<\langle \alpha, v\rangle<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right)\quad \forall \alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}\right\}$$
such that each point $x\in U$ corresponds to a distinct saturated $p$-valuation $\omega_x$ on $I$ given by the Moy-Prasad filtration at the point $x$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
There is a natural isomorphism of filtered Lie $\mathbb{Z}_p$-algebras
$$L_\omega(G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+})_{\frac1{p-1}+}\cong \mathfrak g_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}.$$
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
The Moy-Prasad isomorphisms
$$\mathrm{MP}_{x,r,r+}: G_{x,r}/G_{x,r+}\xrightarrow{\sim} \mathfrak g_{x,r}/\mathfrak g_{x,r+}$$
for $r>\frac1{p-1}$ fit together to form an isomorphism of Lie $\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]$-algebras
\begin{equation}\mathrm{MP}: \operatorname{gr} G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}\xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{gr} \mathfrak g_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}.\end{equation}

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $G$ be any group.  A \textbf{$p$-valuation} on $G$ is a real-valued function
$$\omega:G\setminus\{1\}\to (0,\infty),$$
along with the convention that $\omega(1)=\infty$, satisfying the following four axioms for any $g,h\in G$:
\begin{enumerate}[{(a)}]
\item $\omega(g)>\frac1{p-1}$,
\item $\omega(g^{-1} h)\geq \min\{\omega(g),\omega(h)\}$,
\item $\omega\left([g,h]\right)\geq \omega(g)+\omega(h)$,
\item $\omega(g^p)=\omega(g)+1$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: pth
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pth}
Let $G$ be a group admitting a $p$-valuation $\omega$.  Then the $p$th power map $G\to G$, $g\mapsto g^p$ is injective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By \cite[Proposition 25.1]{schneiderbook}, we know for any $g,h\in G$ that $\omega(g^{-p}h^p)=\omega(g^{-1} h)+1$.  If $g,h\in G$ satisfy $g^p=h^p$, then $\omega(g^{-1} h)=-1+\omega(g^{-p}h^p)=\infty$, which implies that $g=h$.

title: Definition
body_md: $(G,\omega)$ is called \textbf{saturated} if any $g\in G$ such that $\omega(g)>\frac p{p-1}$ is a $p$th power in $G$.

label: OKbasis
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{OKbasis}
(This is similar to \cite[Example 3.4]{LS}).  Let $K/\mathbb{Q}_p$ be a finite extension equipped with the usual valuation $v$ normalized by $v(p)=1$, and fix any $a>\frac1{p-1}$.  Then it follows immediately from the definition that there is a $p$-valuation $\omega$ on $\mathcal O_K$ defined by $\omega(x)\coloneqq v(x)+a$.  Moreover, $(\mathcal O_K,\omega)$ is saturated if and only if
$$a\leq \frac1{e_K}+\frac1{p-1},$$
where $e_K=e(K/\mathbb{Q}_p)$ is the absolute ramification degree of $K$.  Indeed, if $x\in \mathcal O_K$ satisfies $\omega(x)> \frac{p}{p-1}$, then
$$v(x)=\omega(x)-a> \frac{p}{p-1}-a\geq \frac{p}{p-1}-\frac1{p-1}-\frac1{e_K}=1-\frac1{e_K}.$$
Because $v$ takes values in $\frac1{e_K}\mathbb{Z}$, if $v(x)>1-\frac1{e_K}$, it follows that $v(x)\geq 1$.  It is then immediate that there exists some $y\in \mathcal O_K$ such that $x=py$, so indeed $(\mathcal O_K,\omega)$ is saturated.  Conversely, if $a> \frac1{e_K}+\frac1{p-1}$, then choosing $x=\varpi_K^{e_K-1}$ for $\varpi_K\in \mathcal O_K$ a uniformizer gives us an element of $\mathcal O_K$ which is not a multiple of $p$, but which satisfies $\omega(x)> \frac{p}{p-1}$.

          

We note that $(b_1,\ldots, b_\ell)$ is an ordered basis of $(\mathcal O_K,\omega)$ (for any choice of $a>\frac1{p-1}$, so we need not specify in the future) if and only if $(b_i)_{i\leq \ell}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-basis of $\mathcal O_K$ satisfying the equality
$$v\left(\sum_{i=1}^\ell x_ib_i\right)=\min_{i\leq \ell} \{v(b_i)+v(x_i)\}$$
for all $x_i\in \mathbb{Z}_p$.  In such a scenario, we will simply call $(b_i)_{i\leq \ell}$ an \textbf{ordered basis for} $\mathcal O_K$.

label: traceless
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{traceless}
Say $p> 2$.  Let $K/\mathbb{Q}_p$ be a finite extension, and let $E/K$ be a quadratic extension with unique nontrivial Galois automorphism denoted by $x\mapsto \overline x$.  Recall that for any $x\in E$, its \textbf{trace} is defined by $x+\overline x$.  Fix an ordered basis $(b_1,\ldots, b_\ell)$ for $\mathcal O_K$, and let $\gamma\in \mathcal O_E$ be such that $\{1,\gamma\}$ forms an $\mathcal O_K$-basis of $\mathcal O_E$.  If $\gamma$ is \textbf{traceless}, i.e., if $\gamma+\overline \gamma=0$, then 
$$v(x+y\gamma)=\min\{v(x),v(y\gamma)\}$$
for all $x,y\in K$.  Moreover, $(b_1,\ldots, b_\ell,b_1\gamma, \ldots, b_\ell\gamma)$ is an ordered basis of $\mathcal O_E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first claim for any $x,y\in K$ that if $\alpha\coloneqq x+y\gamma$,
$$v(\alpha)=\min\{v(x),v(y)+v(\gamma)\}.$$
Recall that it is always the case that $v(\overline \alpha)=v(\alpha)$, so 
\begin{equation*}
v(\alpha)\leq v(\alpha+\overline\alpha)=v(x+\overline x+y\gamma+\overline{y\gamma})=v(x+y\gamma+x-y\gamma)=v(x),
                            
           
         
\end{equation*}
where the last equality follows from $p> 2$.  Similarly, 
$$v(\alpha)\leq v(\alpha-\overline\alpha)=v(y\gamma),$$
hence $v(x+y\gamma)\leq \min\{v(x), v(y\gamma)\}$.  But the opposite inequality is merely the strong triangle inequality, so indeed $v(x+y\gamma)=\min\{v(x),v(y\gamma)\}$ for any $x,y\in \mathcal O_K$.  The rest of the result follows immediately from $(b_1,\ldots, b_\ell)$ being an ordered basis of $\mathcal O_K$, and $\{1,\gamma\}$ forming an $\mathcal O_K$-basis of $\mathcal O_E$.
head: environment

label: tracelessexistence
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{tracelessexistence}
We remark that so long as $p> 2$, it is always possible to produce a traceless $\gamma\in \mathcal O_E$ such that $\{1,\gamma\}$ forms an $\mathcal O_K$-basis of $\mathcal O_E$.  Indeed, first choose any $\gamma_0\in \mathcal O_E$ such that $\{1,\gamma_0\}$ is an $\mathcal O_K$-basis.  Let $\mathrm{tr}(\gamma_0)$ denote the trace of $\gamma_0$, which lies in $\mathcal O_K$.  If we set $\gamma\coloneqq \gamma_0-\frac12\mathrm{tr}(\gamma_0)\in \mathcal O_E$, then it follows that $\{1,\gamma\}$ is still an $\mathcal O_K$-basis of $\mathcal O_E$, and by construction $\gamma$ is traceless.

label: invariants
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{invariants}
Let $(G,\omega)$ be a saturated pro-$p$ group.  Let $\theta:G\to G$ be any group homomorphism.  If we define $G^\theta\coloneqq \{g\in G\,|\,\theta(g)=g\}$, which is always a subgroup of $G$, then $(G^\theta,\omega|_{G^\theta})$ is saturated.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first note that because $G$ is pro-$p$ and of finite rank, the homomorphism $\theta:G\to G$ is automatically continuous by \cite[Corollary 1.21]{DDMS}.  Thus, $G^\theta$ is a closed subgroup of $G$, so is also of finite rank.

Suppose now that $h\in G^\theta$ is such that $\omega(h)>\frac p{p-1}$.  Since $(G,\omega)$ is saturated, this implies that there is some $g\in G$ such that $g^p=h$.  We then find that 
$$\theta(g)^p=\theta(g^p)=\theta(h)=h=g^p.$$
Because taking $p$th powers in a $p$-valuable group is injective by Proposition \ref{pth}, this implies that $\theta(g)=g$.  Therefore, $g\in G^\theta$ is such that $g^p=h$, so we conclude that $G^\theta$ is saturated.

label: grG
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{grG}
For any real number $v>0$, we write
$$G_v\coloneqq \{g\in G\,|\,\omega(g)\geq v\}\quad \mathrm{and}\quad G_{v+}\coloneqq \{g\in G\,|\,\omega(g)>v\}.$$
These are normal subgroups of $G$, and form a decreasing exhaustive separated filtration of $G$ satisfying $[G_v,G_{v'}]\subseteq G_{v+v'}$ for all $v,v'>0$.  For each $v>0$, define $\operatorname{gr}_v G\coloneqq G_v/G_{v+}$, which is an abelian group.  We then define the associated graded abelian group
$$\operatorname{gr} G\coloneqq \bigoplus_{v>0} \operatorname{gr}_v G.$$
As in \cite{dottolehung}, we write $\mathrm{symb}(g)\in \operatorname{gr} G$ for the homogeneous element in $\operatorname{gr}_{\omega(g)}G$ which is the image of $g$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
As explained in \cite[Section 25]{schneiderbook}, $\operatorname{gr} G$ is naturally an $\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]$-Lie algebra, where 
$$[\mathrm{symb}(g),\mathrm{symb}(h)]=[g,h]G_{\omega(g)+\omega(h)}$$
for $g,h\in G$, and $\varepsilon(\mathrm{symb}(g))=g^p G_{\omega(g)+1}=\mathrm{symb}(g^p)$.  Moreover, this is a free $\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]$-module: given an ordered basis $(g_1,\ldots, g_r)$ of $(G,\omega)$, we have an $\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]$-basis of $\operatorname{gr} G$ given by $\left(\mathrm{symb}(g_i)\right)_{i\leq r}$.

label: log-exp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{log-exp}
Assume $G$ is saturated.  The filtration-preserving $\log$ and $\exp$ induce well-defined mutually inverse isomorphisms of Lie $\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]$-algebras
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\operatorname{gr} L_\omega(G)_{\frac1{p-1}+}=\bigoplus_{v>\frac1{p-1}} L_\omega(G)_v/L_\omega(G)_{v+}} & \bigoplus_{v>\frac1{p-1}}G_v/G_{v+}=\operatorname{gr} G.
	\arrow["\operatorname{gr}\exp", shift left=2, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\operatorname{gr}\log", shift left=2, from=1-2, to=1-1]
\end{tikzcd}\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will show that $\operatorname{gr} \log$ is well-defined, $\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]$-linear, and preserves the Lie bracket; one can easily show using similar arguments that the same holds for $\operatorname{gr} \exp$.

By construction, $\operatorname{gr}\log$ is the direct sum of the homogeneous maps 
$$\operatorname{gr}_v\log:G_v/G_{v+}\to L_\omega(G)_v/L_\omega(G)_{v+}$$
defined by taking any representative $g\in G_v$ of a coset, and setting $\operatorname{gr}_v\log(g)$ to be the coset $\log(g)+L_\omega(G)_{v+}$, which a priori need not be well-defined.  However, this follows from the following fact: given any $g,h\in G$, 
$$\tilde\omega\left(\log(gh)-\log(g)-\log(h)\right)>\max\{\omega(g),\omega(h)\}.$$
Indeed, if $g\in G_v$ and $h\in G_{v+}$, then $\log(h)\in L_\omega(G)_{v+}$, so this fact implies that $\log(gh)-\log(g)\in L_\omega(G)_{v+}$.  This fact similarly immediately proves that each $\operatorname{gr}_v\log$ is $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear.

To prove this fact, we note that an easy inductive argument using both parts of \cite[Proposition 25.1]{schneiderbook} shows for any $n\geq 1$ that
\begin{equation}\label{25.1gen}
\omega(h^{-p^n}g^{-p^n}(gh)^{p^n})>\max\{\omega(g),\omega(h)\}+n.\end{equation}
We also have by \cite[III.2.1.10]{lazard65} that one can compute $\log(x)+\log(y)$ for $x,y\in G$ by letting $a_n\in G$ for $n\geq 1$ be the unique elements satisfying $a_n^{p^n}=x^{p^n}y^{p^n}$ (which exist and are unique by the saturation of $G$), noting that $(a_n)_n$ is a convergent sequence in $G$ say with limit $a\in G$, in which case $\log(a)$ is the desired value.  To ease notation, one can write this as
$$\log(x)+\log(y)=\log\left(\lim_{n\to \infty}\left(x^{p^n}y^{p^n}\right)^{1/p^n}\right).$$

It follows that
\begin{align*}
\log(gh)-\log(g)-\log(h)&=\log(h^{-1})+\log(g^{-1})+\log(gh)
                                                                                        
\end{align*}
has by \ref{25.1gen} valuation equal to
\begin{align*}
                                         
\lim_{n\to \infty} \omega\left(\left(h^{-p^n}g^{-p^n}(gh)^{p^n}\right)^{1/p^n}\right)
&=\lim_{n\to \infty}\omega(h^{-p^n}g^{-p^n}(gh)^{p^n})-n\\
&>\max\{\omega(g),\omega(h)\}.
\end{align*}
(The inequality remains strict despite the limit due to the values attained by $\omega$ being a discrete set.)  We have thus shown that $\operatorname{gr}\log$ is well-defined and $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear; that it is $\mathbb{F}_p[\varepsilon]$-linear follows from \cite[Lemma 31.1]{schneiderbook}, as we know that $\log(g^x)=x\log(g)$ for any $g\in G$, $x\in \mathbb{Z}_p$.

What remains is to prove that $\operatorname{gr}\log$ preserves the Lie bracket.  Using \cite[Exercice III.2.1.10]{lazard65} and the same shorthand as before, we have for any $g,h\in G$
$$[\log(g),\log(h)]\coloneqq \log(g)\log(h)-\log(h)\log(g)=\log\left(\lim_{n\to \infty}[g^{p^n},h^{p^n}]^{1/p^{2n}}\right).$$
Thus, one can compute that
$$\tilde\omega\left(\log([g,h])-[\log(g),\log(h)]\right)=\lim_{n\to \infty} \omega\left([g,h]^{p^{2n}}[g^{p^n},h^{p^n}]^{-1}\right)-2n,$$
which for any value of $n$ is strictly greater than $\omega(g)+\omega(h)$ by a repeated application of \cite[Proposition 25.3]{schneiderbook}.  As usual, this strict inequality also holds in the limit by the discreteness of $\omega$, proving immediately that the Lie bracket is preserved by $\operatorname{gr}\log$.

label: limits
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{limits}
Let $(\omega_n)_{n\geq 1}$ be a sequence of $p$-valuations on a pro-$p$ group $G$.  Suppose that $(\omega_n(g))_{n\geq 1}$ is a convergent sequence, bounded away from $\frac1{p-1}$, for each $g\in G$.  Then $\omega(g)\coloneqq\lim_{n\to \infty} \omega_n(g)$ defines a $p$-valuation on $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since every $(\omega_n(g))_n$ is bounded away from $\frac1{p-1}$ and convergent, then each $\omega(g)$ lies in $\left(\frac1{p-1},\infty\right)$.  The remaining pieces of the definition of being a $p$-valuation follow immediately from taking limits.

title: Notation
body_md:
Let $p>2$.  Let $G$ be any connected reductive quasisplit group defined over a fixed finite extension $K/\mathbb{Q}_p$.  Pick a maximally $K$-split maximal $K$-torus $T\leq G$, with $S\leq T$ its maximal $K$-split subtorus; since $G$ is quasisplit, $T$ is the centralizer of $S$ in $G$.  Let $(X^*(S),\Phi, X_*(S), \Phi^\vee)$ be its associated relative root datum.  We also let $(X^*(T),\tilde\Phi, X_*(T),\tilde\Phi^\vee)$ denote the absolute root datum.  We also fix compatible systems of positive and simple relative/absolute roots: $\Phi^+\subseteq \Phi$, $\tilde\Phi^+\subseteq \tilde\Phi$, $\Delta\subseteq \Phi^+$, and $\tilde\Delta\subseteq \tilde\Phi^+$.  In particular, we have a $\Theta\coloneqq \mathrm{Gal}(\overline K/K)$-action on $\tilde\Phi$, and we can choose everything so that $\tilde\Delta$ is $\Theta$-invariant, and hence corresponds to a Borel $K$-subgroup $B\leq G$ containing $T$.

For each $\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi$, we let $K_{\tilde\alpha}/K$ be the minimal finite extension over which $\tilde\alpha$ is defined; more concretely, take the stabilizer $\Theta_{\tilde\alpha}$ of $\tilde\alpha$, and let $K_{\tilde\alpha}$ denote its fixed field.

Since $G$ is quasisplit, we have a projection map $\tilde\Phi\twoheadrightarrow \Phi$ given by restriction to $S$, and the preimage of any element of $\Phi$ is a $\Theta$-orbit of an element in $\tilde\Phi$.  In particular, if $\alpha\in \Phi$, different choices of $\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi$ lying above $\alpha$ have fields of definitions $K_{\tilde\alpha}$ which are Galois conjugates.

For each $\alpha\in \Phi$, there is an associated unipotent root $K$-subgroup $U_\alpha$ normalized by $S$ whose Lie algebra is the direct sum of the weight spaces for the action of $S$ on $\mathrm{Lie}(G)$ which are $\mathbb{Z}^+$-multiples of $\alpha$.  (That is, if $\alpha$ is multipliable, we by convention take $U_{2\alpha}\subseteq U_\alpha$.). Similarly, for $\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi$, we can define a unipotent $K_{\tilde\alpha}$-subgroup $U_{\tilde\alpha}$ normalized by $T$ in the same way.

Given our tori $S\leq T\leq G$, we induce tori $S_\mathrm{ad}\leq T_\mathrm{ad}\leq G_\mathrm{ad}$, $S_\mathrm{der}\leq T_\mathrm{der}\leq G_\mathrm{der}$, and $S_\mathrm{sc}\leq T_\mathrm{sc}\leq G_\mathrm{sc}$ which are maximal $K$-split tori and maximally $K$-split maximal tori respectively, given by taking the image of our tori under $G\to G_\mathrm{ad}$, intersecting our tori with $G_\mathrm{der}\leq G$, and taking the preimage of our tori under the composition $G_\mathrm{sc}\to G_\mathrm{der} \to G$.

By \cite[Section 2.6(a)]{KP}, the absolute (resp., relative) root systems of $G$ are naturally identified with those of $G_\mathrm{ad}$, $G_\mathrm{der}$, and $G_\mathrm{sc}$ via the natural maps
$$G_\mathrm{sc}\to G_\mathrm{der}\to G\to G_\mathrm{ad}.$$
Thus, we will not distinguish between any of these in our notation.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
(See \cite[pp. 96-97]{KP}.)  Let $\alpha\in \Phi$.  We say $\alpha$ is \textbf{multipliable} if $2\alpha\in \Phi$, and \textbf{divisible} if there is some $\beta\in \Phi$ such that $\alpha=2\beta$.  We will classify the elements of $\Phi$ into three types as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\alpha$ is of type R1 if it is neither multipliable nor divisible.
\item $\alpha$ is of type R2 if it is multipliable.
\item $\alpha$ is of type R3 if it is divisible.
\end{itemize}
We write $\Phi^{\mathrm{nd}}$ for the set of nondivisible roots, i.e., those of type R1 or R2.  This classification allows us to describe $U_\alpha(K)$ rather explicitly.

label: Chev-Stein-isoms
title: Remark
head: environment

label: root-filts
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{root-filts}
Our Chevalley-Steinberg system $X$ induces in the usual way (e.g., see \cite[Construction 6.1.17]{KP}) a Chevalley valuation of the root datum, which is an absolutely special point $x_0$ of the semisimple apartment $\mathcal A(S)$ of $G$ associated to $S$ by \cite[Proposition 7.11.4]{KP}.  We can translate $x_0$ by any element of the vector space $V(S)\coloneqq \mathbb{R}\otimes_\mathbb{Z} X_*(S)$; this action factors through $V(A_G)$ for $A_G\leq G$ the maximal $K$-split torus in the center of $G$ (see \cite[p. 200]{KP}), giving in fact an action of $V(S/A_G)$.  Now $S/A_G$ is isogenous to a maximal $K$-split torus $S_\mathrm{ad}$ in $T_\mathrm{ad}$, the image of $T$ in $G_\mathrm{ad}$, which is a maximally split maximal $K$-torus.  Thus, 
$$V(S)/V(A_G)=V(S/A_G)=V(S_\mathrm{ad})=V(T_\mathrm{ad})^\Theta.$$
In fact, $\mathcal A(S)$ is an affine space over these equal vector spaces.  Given any $x\in \mathcal A(S)$, we have an associated filtration on the root groups given as follows.  (Note that $U_{\alpha,x,r}$ is used in two different ways in \cite{KP}; our notation agrees with \cite[7.3.3]{KP} with the constant function $f=r$, but disagrees with \cite[6.1.2]{KP}.)  Note that there is a unique $v\in V(S_\mathrm{ad})$ such that $x=x_0+v$.



If $\alpha\in \Phi$ is of type R1, then for $r\geq 0$,
$$U_{\alpha,x,r}=\{u_\alpha(x)\,|\, x\in K_{\tilde\alpha}, v(x)+\langle \alpha,v\rangle\geq r\}.$$
We also write 
$$U_{\alpha,x,r+}=\bigcup_{s>r} U_{\alpha, x, s}=\{u_\alpha(x)\,|\, x\in K_{\tilde\alpha}, v(x)+\langle \alpha,v\rangle> r\}.$$
If $\alpha\in \Phi$ is of type R2, then we have for $r\geq 0$ the filtration
$$U_{\alpha,x,r}= \Big\{u_\alpha(x,y)\,\Big|\, x,y\in K_{\tilde\alpha}, x\overline x=y+\overline y, \quad \min\{v(x)+\langle \alpha,v\rangle, v(y)+2\langle \alpha,v\rangle\}\geq r\Big\}.$$
We also have
\begin{align*}
U_{\alpha,x,r+}&= \bigcup_{s>r} U_{\alpha,x,s}\\
&=\Big\{u_\alpha(x,y)\,\Big|\, x,y\in K_{\tilde\alpha}, x\overline x=y+\overline y, \quad \min\{v(x)+\langle \alpha,v\rangle, v(y)+2\langle \alpha,v\rangle\}> r\Big\}.
\end{align*}

label: root-group-pval
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{root-group-pval}
Let $x\in \mathcal A(S)$ be arbitrary, and assume $p> 2$.  For $u\in U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$, define
$$\omega(u)\coloneqq \min\left\{r>\frac1{p-1} \,\Bigg|\, u\in U_{\alpha,x,r}\right\}.$$
Then $\omega$ is a $p$-valuation on $U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$, and moreover it is saturated.

label: OKsaturation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{OKsaturation}
Let $F/\mathbb{Q}_p$ be any finite extension.  Let $a\in \mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary, and let $i$ be the least integer strictly greater than
$$e_F\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-a\right),$$
so that $\mathfrak m_F^i=\{x\in F\,|\, v(x)>\frac1{p-1}-a\}$.  Then the function $\omega$ on $\mathfrak m_F^i$ defined by
$$\omega(x)\coloneqq v(x)+a$$
is a saturated $p$-valuation.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that our valuation is normalized so that $v(p)=1$, so the only nontrivial part of verifying that this is a $p$-valuation is checking that $\omega(x)>\frac1{p-1}$; this follows from the choice of $i$, as
$$\omega(x)=v(x)+a\geq \frac i{e_F}+a>\frac1{p-1}$$
for any $x\in \mathfrak m_F^i$.  

To see that it is a saturated $p$-valuation, suppose that $x\in \mathfrak m_F^i$ is not a $p$th power (i.e., not a multiple of $p$), which directly implies that $x\notin \mathfrak m_F^{i+e_F}$, or in other words that
$$v(x)<\frac{i}{e_F}+1.$$
Thus, as $v(x)\in \frac1{e_F}\mathbb{Z}$, we know that $v(x)\leq \frac{i-1}{e_F}+1$.  It follows then from our choice of $i$ that
$$\omega(x)=v(x)+a\leq \frac1{p-1}+1=\frac{p}{p-1},$$
as otherwise we could have chosen a smaller value of $i$, so $\omega$ is indeed saturated.
head: environment

label: R2-desc
title: Remark
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: The function $\omega$ defines a $p$-valuation on $U_{\alpha}^a$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $a\in \mathbb{Q}$.  By a mild generalization of \cite[Example 23.3]{schneiderbook} using the exact same argument, one can construct a $p$-valuation on the standard pro-$p$ Iwahori subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal O_E)$ given that $ne<p-1$.  (This is also \cite[III.3.2.7]{lazard65}.)  However, the only requirement for that proof to go through for a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$ consisting of upper triangular unipotent matrices is that $(j-i)a+v(a_{ij})>\frac1{p-1}$ for any $i<j$, i.e., in our case that $v(x)+a>\frac1{p-1}$ and $v(y)+2a>\frac1{p-1}$ for $u_\alpha(x,y)\in U_{\alpha}^a$.  If this condition is satisfied, the claimed function is immediately shown to be a $p$-valuation.  This property follows directly from our above description of $U_{\alpha}^a$.  One can then use Lemma \ref{limits} to allow $a$ to lie outside of $\mathbb{Q}$: letting $i$ and $j$ be the integers in Remark \ref{R2-desc}, any $a'$ satisfying
$$a\geq a'>\max\left\{\frac1{p-1}-\frac{i}{e_E}, \frac12\left(\frac1{p-1}-\frac{j}{e_E}\right)\right\}$$
will have $U_\alpha^{a'}=U_\alpha^a$.  (The definitions of $i$ and $j$ force this interval to be nonempty.)  Now choose a sequence of such $a'$ which are rational and converging to $a$, and then apply Lemma \ref{limits}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $H$ be a $p$-valuable group and let $(H_1,\ldots, H_s)$ be a list of subgroups such that the multiplication map
$$m:H_1\times\cdots\times H_s\to H$$
is bijective.  We say a $p$-valuation $\omega$ on $H$ is \textbf{compatible} with $(H_1,\ldots H_s)$ if 
$$\omega(h_1\cdots h_s)=\min\{\omega(h_1),\ldots, \omega(h_s)\}$$
for all $h_i\in H_i$.
head: environment

label: compatibility
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is easy to check that these are indeed all closed subgroups of $U_\alpha^a$, so we will omit this.  In fact, each is isomorphic to $\mathfrak m_F^n$ as a topological group for appropriate values of $n$, via the respective maps $x\mapsto u_\alpha\left(x,\frac12x^2\right)$, $y\mapsto u_\alpha\left(y\gamma,-\frac12y^2\gamma^2\right)$, and $z\mapsto u_\alpha(0,z\gamma)$.  Concretely, if we write $n_1,n_2,n_3$ for the least integers strictly greater than 
$$e_F\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-a\right),\qquad e_F\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-a-v(\gamma)\right),\qquad e_F\cdot\left( \frac1{p-1}-2a-v(\gamma)\right),$$
respectively, then we have isomorphisms $\mathfrak m_F^{n_i}\xrightarrow{\sim} U_{\alpha,i}^a$ for each $1\leq i \leq 3$.


First, we will show that the multiplication map is bijective; it is sufficient to show that the composition $\phi:\mathfrak m_F^{n_1}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_2}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_3}\to U_{\alpha}^a$ of the multiplication map with the above three isomorphisms is a bijection.  A brief computation reveals that $\phi$ is explicitly given by
\begin{align*}
\phi:\mathfrak m_F^{n_1}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_2}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_3}&\to G\\
(x,y,z)&\mapsto u_\alpha\left(x,\frac12x^2\right)\cdot u_\alpha\left(y\gamma,-\frac12y^2\gamma^2\right)\cdot u_\alpha(0,z\gamma)\\
&\qquad=u_\alpha\left(x+y\gamma, \frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z-xy)\right).
\end{align*}
Suppose that $\phi(x,y,z)=\phi(x',y',z')$, so that
\begin{align*}
x+y\gamma&=x'+y'\gamma,\\
\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z-xy)&=\frac12(x'^2-y'^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z'-x'y').
\end{align*}
Recall that $\{1,\gamma\}$ is an $\mathcal O_F$-basis of $\mathcal O_E$ (and in particular an $F$-basis of $E$); from this fact, it follows easily that $(x,y,z)=(x',y',z')$.  This proves injectivity.

For surjectivity, fix any $s,t\in E$ such that $s\overline s=t+\overline t$ which satisfy $v(s)>\frac1{p-1}-a$, $v(t)>\frac1{p-1}-2a$, so $u_\alpha(s,t)\in U_\alpha^a$ is an arbitrary element.  There exist $x,y\in F$ such that $s=x+y\gamma$, which by Lemma \ref{traceless} satisfy the equality
$$\min\{v(x),v(y)+v(\gamma)\}=v(s)>\frac1{p-1}-a.$$
Similarly, there are $w_0,z_0\in F$ such that $t=w_0+z_0\gamma$, which then satisfy
$$\min\{v(w_0), v(z_0)+v(\gamma)\}=v(t)>\frac1{p-1}-2a.$$
We then get directly from $s\overline s=t+\overline t$ that $w_0=\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)$.  Now, let $z\coloneqq z_0+xy$, and note from our above information on the valuations of our elements that
$$v(x)>\frac1{p-1}-a,\qquad v(y)>\frac1{p-1}-a-v(\gamma),\qquad\text{and } v(z_0)>\frac1{p-1}-2a-v(\gamma),$$
so 
\begin{align*}
v(z)&\geq \min\{v(z_0),v(x)+v(y)\}\\
&>\min\left\{\frac1{p-1}-2a-v(\gamma),\frac2{p-1}-2a-v(\gamma)\right\}\\
&=\frac1{p-1}-2a-v(\gamma).
\end{align*}
Thus, $(x,y,x)\in \mathfrak m_F^{n_1}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_2}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_3}$, so we can conclude that
$$\phi(x,y,z)=u_\alpha\left(x+y\gamma, \frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z-xy)\right)=u_\alpha(s,t),$$
finishing the proof that $\phi:\mathfrak m_F^{n_1}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_2}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_3}\to U_\alpha^a$ is bijective.  The multiplication map $U_{\alpha,1}^a\times U_{\alpha,2}^a\times U_{\alpha,3}^a\to U_\alpha^a$ must hence also be bijective.

Next, we must check that $\omega$ is compatible with $(U_{\alpha,1}^a,U_{\alpha,2}^a,U_{\alpha,3}^a)$, i.e., that
$$\omega(g_1g_2g_3)=\min\{\omega(g_1),\omega(g_3),\omega(g_3)\}$$
for any $g_i\in U_{\alpha,i}^a$.  Due to our bounds on the valuations of $(x,y,z)\in \mathfrak m_F^{n_1}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_2}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_3}$, one can check that 
$$\omega\left(u_\alpha\left(x, \frac12x^2\right)\right)=v(x)+a,\qquad \omega\left(u_\alpha\left(y\gamma, \frac12y^2\gamma^2\right)\right)=v(y)+v(\gamma)+a,$$ 
$$\omega\left(u_\alpha(0,z\gamma)\right)=v(z)+v(\gamma)+2a.$$
Thus, our requirement translates to checking for all $(x,y,z)\in \mathfrak m_F^{n_1}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_2}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_3}$ that
$$\omega(g)=\min\{v(x)+a, v(y)+v(\gamma)+a, v(z)+v(\gamma)+ 2a\},$$
where
$$g=\phi(x,y,z)=u_\alpha\left(x+y\gamma, \frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z-xy)\right).$$
Since $v(x+\gamma y)=\min\{v(x),v(y)+v(\gamma)\}$ by Lemma \ref{traceless}, this is equivalent to checking that
$$\omega(g)=\min\{a+v(x+y\gamma),2a+v(\gamma z)\}.$$
By definition, we already know that
$$\omega(g)=\min\left\{a+v(x+y\gamma),2a+v\left(\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z-xy)\right)\right\}.$$
Assume that 
$$v(\gamma z)\neq v\left(\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z-xy)\right),$$
which is the only possible situation where the above two minima could differ; we will prove in this case that $a+v(x+y\gamma)$ attains both minima, hence they are equal.  This assumption implies automatically that
$$v\left(\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)-xy\gamma\right)\leq v(\gamma z),$$
which we first claim implies $v(x+y\gamma)<a+v(\gamma z)$.  By Lemma \ref{traceless}, as $\gamma^2\in \mathcal O_F$, we know that
\begin{align*}
v\left(\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)-xy\gamma\right)&=\min\left\{v\left(\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)\right), v(xy\gamma)\right\}\\
&=\min\{2v(x+y\gamma), v(x)+v(y\gamma)\},
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows from $p\neq 2$ and $x^2-y^2\gamma^2=(x+y\gamma)(\overline{x+y\gamma})$.  If $2v(x+y\gamma)\leq v(\gamma z)$, then 
$$v(x+y\gamma)\leq -v(x+y\gamma)+v(\gamma z)<a-\frac1{p-1}+v(\gamma z)<a+v(\gamma z).$$
Similarly, if $v(x)+v(y\gamma)\leq v(\gamma z)$, then 
$$v(x)\leq -v(y\gamma)+v(\gamma z)<a-\frac1{p-1} +v(\gamma z)<a+v(\gamma z).$$
This would imply that
$$v(x+y\gamma)=\min\{v(x),v(y\gamma)\}\leq v(x)<a+v(\gamma z),$$
so we have in all cases from our assumption that $v(x+y\gamma)<a+v(\gamma z)$.  Thus, we need only verify under our assumption that $\omega(g)=a+v(x+y\gamma)$, i.e., that
$$v(x+y\gamma)\leq a+v\left(\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)+\gamma(z-xy)\right).$$
Again, by Lemma \ref{traceless}, the latter is given by
$$a+\min\left\{v\left(\frac12(x^2-y^2\gamma^2)\right), v(\gamma(z-xy)\right\}=a+\min\{2v(x+y\gamma), v(\gamma(z-xy))\},$$
so it is sufficient to show that $v(x+y\gamma)\leq a+ v(\gamma(z-xy))$.  We know $v(\gamma(z-xy))\geq \min\{v(\gamma z), v(xy\gamma)\}$ and $a+v(\gamma z)>v(x+y\gamma)$, so it is sufficient to check that $v(xy\gamma)+a>v(x+y\gamma)$.  Indeed, 
$$v(xy\gamma)=v(x)+v(y\gamma)>v(x)+\frac1{p-1}-a>v(x)-a$$
so
$$v(x+y\gamma)=\min\{v(x),v(y\gamma)\}<v(xy\gamma)+a$$
as claimed.  This completes the proof that $\omega$ is compatible with $(U_{\alpha,1}^a, U_{\alpha,2}^a, U_{\alpha,3}^a)$.
head: environment

label: compatible-saturation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{compatible-saturation}
Suppose that $H$ is a $p$-valuable group, and $\omega$ is a $p$-valuation on $H$ compatible with a list of subgroups $(H_1,\ldots, H_s)$ as above.  If $(b_{i,1},\ldots, b_{i,t_i})$ is an ordered basis of $(H_i,\omega|_{H_i})$ for each $i\leq s$, then we can produce an ordered basis for $H$ given by 
$$(b_{1,1},\ldots, b_{1,t_1},\quad b_{2,1},\ldots, b_{2,t_2},\quad \ldots, \quad b_{s,1},\ldots, b_{s,t_s}).$$
In particular, if each $(H_i,\omega|_{H_i})$ is saturated, then $\omega(b_{i,j})\leq \frac p{p-1}$ for all $i\leq s$, $j\leq t_i$, from which it follows that also $(H,\omega)$ is saturated.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: The $p$-valuation $\omega$ on $U_\alpha^a$ is saturated.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that we have isomorphisms $\phi_j:\mathfrak m_F^{n_k}\xrightarrow{\sim} U_{\alpha,j}^a$ for each $1\leq j\leq 3$, and
$$\omega(\phi_1(x))=v(x)+a,\qquad \omega(\phi_2(y))=v(y)+v(\gamma)+a,\qquad \omega(\phi_3(z))=v(z)+v(\gamma)+2a$$
for all $(x,y,z)\in \mathfrak m_F^{n_1}\times \mathfrak m_F^{n_2}\times\mathfrak m_F^{n_3}$.  Recall that $n_1,n_2,n_3$ denote the least integers strictly greater than 
$$e_F\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-a\right),\qquad e_F\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-a-v(\gamma)\right),\qquad e_F\cdot\left( \frac1{p-1}-2a-v(\gamma)\right),$$
respectively.  Thus, it is immediate from three applications of Lemma \ref{OKsaturation} that $\omega$ restricts to a saturated $p$-valuation on $U_{\alpha, j}^a$ for each $1\leq j \leq 3$, and hence is saturated on $U_\alpha^a$.
head: environment

label: basis
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since our isomorphisms $\phi_j$ between $\mathfrak m_F^{n_j}$ and each of $U_{\alpha, j}^a$ pull $\omega$ back to mere shifts of the standard $p$-valuation on $\mathfrak m_F^{n_j}$, i.e., we have that
$$\omega(\phi_1(x))=v(x)+a,\qquad \omega(\phi_2(y))=v(y)+v(\gamma)+a,\qquad \omega(\phi_3(z))=v(z)+v(\gamma)+2a,$$
then it follows from Remark \ref{OKbasis} that $(\varpi_F^{n_j}b_1,\ldots, \varpi_F^{n_j}b_\ell)$ is an ordered basis for $\mathfrak m_F^{n_j}$ with respect to the $p$-valuations induced by these three isomorphisms.  Thus, their images 
$$(\phi_j(\varpi_F^{n_j}b_1),\ldots, \phi_j(\varpi_F^{n_j}b_\ell))$$
form an ordered basis of $(U_{\alpha,j}^a,\omega)$ for each $1\leq j\leq 3$, and we have that $\phi_j(\varpi_F^{n_j}b_i)=g_{j,i}$ for $1\leq j\leq 3$, $1\leq i\leq \ell$.  By our previous remark, we can thus concatenate to produce the claimed ordered basis of $U_\alpha^a$.
head: environment

label: Gm-log-exp
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Gm-log-exp}
It is a standard result that if $r$ is the smallest integer greater than $e_K/(p-1)$, and $n\geq r$, then $U_K^{(n)}=1+\mathfrak m_K^n$ is saturated with $p$-valuation $\omega(x)=v(x-1)+\frac{r-n}{e_K}$.  This follows from the fact that $\log$ and $\exp$ give isomorphisms $U_K^{(m)}\cong \mathfrak m_K^m$ for any $m\geq r$, and $\mathfrak m_K^n$ has saturated $p$-valuation 
$$\omega_0(x)=v(x)+\frac{r-n}{e_K}$$
for any $n$ due to Lemma \ref{OKsaturation}.
head: environment

title: Note
body_md:
In particular, the above shows that $U_K^{(r)}$ for $r$ the least integer greater than $e_K/(p-1)$ is saturated by
$$\omega(x)=v(x-1).$$
This is also equal to
$$\omega(x)=\frac1{e_K}\cdot \sup\left\{n\in \mathbb{Z}^+\,\Big|\,  x\in U_K^{(n)}\right\}.$$
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The torus $T$ is called \textbf{induced} if there is some $m\in \mathbb{Z}^+$ and there are finite extensions $L_i/K$ for $i\leq m$ such that
$$T\cong \prod_{i=1}^m {R}_{L_i/K}\mathbb{G}_m$$
are isomorphic $K$-tori.

We also say that $T$ is \textbf{weakly induced} if there is a tamely ramified extension $L/K$ such that the base change $T_L$ is an induced torus.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: $T$ is weakly induced if and only if there is a basis of $X^*(T)$ on which the wild inertia subgroup of $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline K/K)$ acts via a permutation action.  (See \cite[p. 669]{KP}.)
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Let $G$ be a quasisplit connected reductive $K$-group, and $T\leq G$ a maximal $K$-torus contained in a Borel $K$-subgroup.  If $G$ is semisimple, as well as either adjoint or simply connected, then $T$ is an induced torus.  (See \cite[p. 86]{KP}.)
head: environment

title: Notation
body_md:
If $T$ is a weakly induced torus, the filtration we use on it is the \textbf{standard filtration} given by $T(K)_0$ the Iwahori subgroup $T(K)^0$, and
$$T(K)_r\coloneqq\{t\in T(K)\,|\,  v(\chi(t)-1)\geq r\text{ for all } \chi\in X^*(T)\}$$
for $r>0$.  The maximal pro-$p$ subgroup of $T(K)$ is given by
$$T(K)_{0+}\coloneqq\{t\in T(K)\,|\, v(\chi(t)-1)>0\text{ for all }\chi\in X^*(T)\}.$$
(For more details, see \cite[pp. 245 \& 692]{KP}.)
head: environment

title: Note
body_md: The appropriate filtration on tori to be using is the minimal congruent filtration introduced by Yu in \cite{yu-smooth_models}.  However, when $T$ is weakly induced, this coincides with the standard filtration by \cite[Corollary B.10.13]{KP}, and is consequently much easier to study; we will work almost exclusively with this case.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Say $T=\prod_{i=1}^m{R}_{L_i/K}\mathbb{G}_m$ (so $T$ is induced).  Then we have the equalities
$$T(K)=\prod_{i=1}^m L_i^\times,\qquad T(K)_0=\prod_{i=1}^m \mathcal O_{L_i}^\times,\qquad T(K)_{0+}=\prod_{i=1}^m U_{L_i}^{(1)}.$$
head: environment

label: split-torus-sat
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{split-torus-sat}
Let $T$ be a split $K$-torus.  Then
$$T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}=\{t\in T(K)\,|\, v(\chi(t)-1)>\frac1{p-1} \text{ for all }\chi\in X^*(T)\}$$
has a natural $p$-valuation given by $\omega(t)=\sup\left\{r\in \left(\frac1{p-1},\infty\right)\,\Big|\, t\in T(K)_r\right\}$.  Moreover, $(T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+},\omega)$ is saturated.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $T$ is split, then $T(K)\cong (K^\times)^m$ for some $m$.  Now $T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}\cong(U_K^{(r)})^m$ where $r$ is the least integer greater than $e_K/(p-1)$, and the function $\omega$ on $T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$ corresponds to the function given on $(x_i)_{i\leq n}\in (U_K^{(r)})^m$ by 
$$\min_{i\leq m} \frac1{e_K}\cdot \sup\{n\in \mathbb{Z}^+\,|\, x_i\in U_K^{(n)}\}=\min_{i\leq m} v(x_i-1).$$
Since $\omega_i(x_i)\coloneqq v(x_i-1)$ is saturated on $U_K^{(r)}$ for each $i$, then it follows easily that $((U_K^{(r)})^m,\omega)$, and hence $(T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+},\omega)$, is also saturated.
head: environment

label: torus-saturation
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{torus-saturation}
Let $T$ be a weakly induced $K$-torus.  Then $T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$ has a natural $p$-valuation given by
$$\omega(t)=\sup\left\{r\in \left(\frac1{p-1},\infty\right)\,\Bigg|\, t\in T(K)_r\right\}.$$
Moreover, $\left(T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+},\omega\right)$ is $p$-saturated.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E/K$ be a finite Galois extension such that the base change $T_E$ is split.  Note that
$$T(K)_r=T(E)_r\cap T(K)=T_E(E)_r^{\mathrm{Gal}(E/K)}$$
for all $r>0$ (see \cite[Remark B.6.8]{KP} or even \cite[Proposition 12.9.4]{KP}), and similarly $T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}=T_E(E)_{\frac1{p-1}+}^{\mathrm{Gal}(E/K)}$.  Thus, the $p$-valuation we have defined on $T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$ is merely the restriction of the one we have defined previously on the split $T_E(E)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$.  This result is now immediate from Lemma \ref{split-torus-sat} and our earlier observation in Proposition \ref{invariants} that if a group is saturated, its subgroup of invariants under a family of homomorphisms is also saturated.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
For any $x\in \mathcal B(G)$, there is a saturated $p$-valuation $\omega$ on $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ defined by
$$\omega(g)=\min\left\{r>\frac1{p-1}\,\Bigg|\, g\in G_{x,r}\right\}.$$
head: environment

label: congruence-pval
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{congruence-pval}
Let $E/\mathbb{Q}_p$ be a finite extension with $e_E=e(E/\mathbb{Q}_p)$, and suppose $\mathcal G$ is an $\mathcal O_E$-subgroup scheme of $\mathrm{GL}_N$ for some $N\in \mathbb{Z}^+$.  For $r\in \mathbb{Z}^+$, consider the congruence subgroup $K_r$ defined by
$$K_r\coloneqq \ker\left(\mathcal G(\mathcal O_E)\to \mathcal G(\mathcal O_E/\mathfrak m_E^r)\right).$$
Then for $r>\frac {e_E}{p-1}$, the expression
$$\omega(g)=\frac1{e_E}\cdot \sup\{n\in \mathbb{Z}^+\,|\, g\in K_n\}$$
defines a $p$-valuation on $K_r$.
head: environment

label: conjlemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{conjlemma}
Suppose that $G$ is quasisplit and $T$ is weakly induced.  Assume that $v\in X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$.  Then there exists a pair $(E,t)$ consisting of a finite extension $E/K$ such that $G_E$ splits and an element $t\in T(E)$ such that $tG_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}t^{-1}\subseteq K_r$, where $r$ is the smallest integer $>e_E/(p-1)$ for $e_E=e(E/\mathbb{Q}_p)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This proof is directly inspired by that of \cite[Lemma 3.2]{LS}.  Pick any lift $\mu_0\in X_*(S)_\mathbb{Q}$ of $v$, so there exists some $n\in \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that $\mu\coloneqq n\mu_0\in X_*(S)=X_*(T)^\Theta$ by clearing denominators.  Pick now $E/K$ large enough such that $G_E$ splits and there is some $c\in E^\times$ with $v(c)=\frac 1n$.  We claim that $t\coloneqq \mu(c)\in T(E)$ suffices.

Indeed, recall that the multiplication map gives a homeomorphism
$$\prod_{\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi^-} U_{\tilde\alpha, x_0,r/e_E}^E\times T(E)_{r/e_E}\times \prod_{\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi^+} U_{\tilde\alpha, x_0,r/e_E}^E\to K_r$$
for any $r\geq 0$.  For each $\alpha\in \Phi$, choose $\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi$ lying above $\alpha$, and if $\alpha$ is of type R2, we also pick $\tilde\alpha'$ above $\alpha$ and $\tilde\beta$ above $2\alpha$ exactly as in Remark \ref{Chev-Stein-isoms}.

Using our Iwahori factorization
$$\prod_{\alpha\in \Phi^{-,\mathrm{nd}}} U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}\times T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}\times\prod_{\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}}U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}\to G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+},$$
and the analogous one above for $K_r$, we see that $tG_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}t^{-1}\subseteq K_r$ can be checked on each Iwahori factor.
\begin{enumerate}[{(i)}]
\item For $\alpha\in \Phi^\mathrm{nd}$ of type R1, 
\begin{align*}
tU_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}t^{-1}\subseteq \prod_{\sigma\in \Theta/\Theta_{\tilde\alpha}}U_{\sigma\tilde\alpha,x_0,r/e_E}^E
&\iff (\sigma\tilde\alpha)(t)\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}\subseteq \mathfrak m_E^r\qquad \forall \sigma\in \Theta
\end{align*}
where $m_\alpha\in \mathbb{Z}$ is the least integer strictly greater than 
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle \alpha, v\rangle\right).$$
Since $t=\mu(c)$, and $\mu_0=\frac1n \mu$ is Galois-invariant, note that 
\begin{align*}
v((\sigma\tilde\alpha)(t))=v((\sigma\tilde\alpha)(\mu(c)))&=v(c^{\langle \sigma\tilde\alpha, \mu\rangle})=\langle \sigma\tilde\alpha, \mu\rangle \cdot v(c)\\
&=\langle \sigma\tilde\alpha, \mu_0\rangle=\langle \tilde\alpha, \sigma^{-1}\mu_0\rangle=\langle \tilde\alpha, \mu_0\rangle=\langle \alpha, v\rangle.
\end{align*}
Thus, $(\sigma\tilde\alpha)(t)m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}\subseteq m_E^r$ is immediate from the description of $m_\alpha$ and $r$ being the least integers strictly greater than 
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle \alpha, v\rangle\right)\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad e_E\cdot \frac1{p-1},$$
respectively.
\item For $\alpha\in \Phi^\mathrm{nd}$ of type R2,
\begin{align*}
tU_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}t^{-1}&\subseteq \prod_{\sigma\in \Theta/\Theta_{\tilde\beta}}U_{\sigma\tilde\alpha,x_0,r/e_E}^E\cdot U_{\sigma\tilde\alpha',x_0,r/e_E}^E\cdot U_{\sigma\tilde\beta,x_0,r/e_E}^E\qquad\\
\iff&(\sigma\tilde\alpha)(t)\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}, \quad (\sigma\tilde\alpha')(t)\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}, \quad (\sigma\tilde\beta)(t)\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{n_\alpha}\quad \subseteq \mathfrak m_E^r\qquad \forall \sigma\in \Theta,
\end{align*}
where $m_\alpha$ and $n_\alpha$ are the least integers strictly greater than 
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle \alpha, v\rangle\right)\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle 2\alpha, v\rangle\right),$$
respectively.  Once again, we can check from $t=\mu(c)$ that
$$v((\sigma\tilde\alpha)(t))=v((\sigma\tilde\alpha')(t))=\langle \alpha, v\rangle$$
and
$$v((\sigma\tilde\beta)(t))=\langle 2\alpha, v\rangle,$$
so as in the last item, our requirement that
$$(\sigma\tilde\alpha)(t)\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}, \quad (\sigma\tilde\alpha')(t)\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}, \quad (\sigma\tilde\beta)(t)\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{n_\alpha}\quad \subseteq \mathfrak m_E^r\qquad \forall \sigma\in \Theta$$
is immediately satisfied as $r$ is the least integer strictly greater than $e_E\cdot \frac1{p-1}$.
\item For the torus, since $T(E)$ is abelian and $T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}\subseteq T(E)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$, it is immediate that
$$tT(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}t^{-1}=T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}\subseteq T(E)_{r/e_E}.$$
\end{enumerate}
Thus, $t=\mu(c)$ indeed satisfies the requirement that $tG_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}t^{-1} \subseteq K_r$.

head: environment

label: density
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{density}
For each $x\in \mathcal A(S)$, there is a subset $Q$ of 
$$x_0+X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}\subseteq \mathcal A(S)$$
either containing $x$ or which has $x$ as a limit point, and which satisfies the requirement that $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}=G_{x',\frac1{p-1}+}$ for all $x'\in Q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using Iwahori factorizations, to conclude that $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}=G_{x',\frac1{p-1}+}$, it is sufficient to show that $U_{\alpha, x, \frac1{p-1}+}=U_{\alpha, x', \frac1{p-1}+}$ for each $\alpha\in \Phi^{\mathrm{nd}}$; equivalently, we need $v'\coloneqq x'-x_0\in X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$ to satisfy
$$U_{\alpha, x_0+v, \frac1{p-1}+}=U_{\alpha, x_0+v', \frac1{p-1}+}$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{\mathrm{nd}}$, where $v=x-x_0$.  Using our usual description of the root groups when written in this form (see Subsection \ref{R1} and Remark \ref{R2-desc}), it is equivalent to show that
$$\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle \alpha, v\rangle\right)\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle \alpha, v'\rangle\right)\right\rfloor$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{\mathrm{nd}}$, and that 
$$\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle 2\alpha, v\rangle\right)\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle 2\alpha, v'\rangle\right)\right\rfloor$$
when $\alpha\in \Phi^{\mathrm{nd}}$ is of type R2.  (Here, $\lfloor s \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer $n$ with $n\leq s$ for any $s\in \mathbb{R}$.)  Since $\langle -\alpha, v'\rangle= -\langle \alpha, v'\rangle$ and $\langle \pm 2\alpha, v'\rangle=\pm2 \langle \alpha, v'\rangle$, we can collect all of these conditions to have the following concise description of a condition on $v'$ for each $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$ which is sufficient to ensure $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}=G_{x',\frac1{p-1}+}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\langle \alpha, v\rangle$ is already rational, we require that $\langle \alpha, v'\rangle=\langle \alpha, v\rangle$.
\item If $\langle \alpha, v\rangle$ is not rational, then there is an open set of values $V_\alpha$ containing $\langle \alpha, v\rangle$ which we require $\langle \alpha, v'\rangle$ to lie in.
\end{enumerate}
If every $\langle \alpha, v\rangle$ is already rational, then $v\in X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$, so we can just take $Q=\{x\}$; assume without loss of generality that this is not the case.  Note that each $\langle \alpha, -\rangle$ is a rational linear functional $X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}\to \mathbb{Q}$, so our argument will boil down to mere linear algebra.

First, let $A$ denote the set of $v'\in X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$ satisfying the condition that $\langle \alpha, v'\rangle=\langle \alpha, v\rangle$ for each $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$ which has $\langle \alpha, v\rangle\in \mathbb{Q}$.  Since each $\langle \alpha, -\rangle$ is a rational linear functional, and these conditions have a mutual solution $v$ in $V(S_\mathrm{ad})=X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{R}$, it is an elementary linear algebra exercise to show that there is at least one solution in $X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$.  Thus, $A$ is an affine subspace of $X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$ over some subspace $W\subseteq X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$.  Write $A_\mathbb{R}$ for the unique affine subspace of $V(S_\mathrm{ad})$ over $W\otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $A_\mathbb{R}\cap X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}=A$, which is easily seen to contain $v$.

We now have, for each $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$ such that $\langle \alpha, v\rangle$ is not already rational, an affine functional $\langle \alpha, -\rangle: A \to \mathbb{Q}$ which we require to attain values within an open set $V_\alpha\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ which contains $\langle \alpha, v\rangle$.  These induce real affine functionals $\langle \alpha, -\rangle: A_\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$; let $V$ denote the open subset of $v'\in A_\mathbb{R}$ satisfying our condition that $\langle \alpha, v'\rangle\in V_\alpha$ for each such $\alpha$, which is nonempty as it contains $v$ itself.  By the density of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, it is immediate that $V\cap A=V\cap X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}\subseteq V(S_\mathrm{ad})$ is nonempty and has $v$ as a limit point.  Thus, if we write $Q=x_0+(V\cap A)$, we find that $Q\subseteq x_0+X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$ is a subset with $x_0$ as a limit point satisfying the requirement that $G_{x,r}=G_{x',r}$ for all $x'\in Q$.

label: existence
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{existence}
Suppose that $G$ is quasisplit and $T$ is weakly induced.  Then for each $x\in \mathcal B(G)$, there exists a unique $p$-valuation $\omega_x$ on $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ satisfying the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont(a)]
\item $\omega$ is compatible with the Iwahori factorization
$$\prod_{\alpha\in \Phi^{-,\mathrm{nd}}}U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}\times T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}\times\prod_{\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}}U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}\xrightarrow{\sim} G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+},$$
where the products are each taken in any (fixed) order.
\item If $\alpha\in \Phi$ is of type R1, then $\omega_x(u_\alpha(x))=v(x)+\langle \alpha,v\rangle$, where $x\in \mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}$ for $m_\alpha$ the least integer strictly greater than 
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle \alpha, v\rangle\right).$$
\item If $\alpha\in \Phi$ is of type R2, then
$$\omega_x(u_\alpha(x,y))=\min\{v(x)+\langle \alpha, v\rangle, v(y)+2\langle \alpha,v\rangle\},$$
where $x\in \mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{m_\alpha}$ and $y\in \mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^{n_\alpha}$ satisfy $x\overline x=y+\overline y$ for $m_\alpha, n_\alpha$ the least integers strictly greater than 
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle \alpha, v\rangle\right)\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-\langle 2\alpha, v\rangle\right),$$
respectively.
\item If $t\in T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$, then 
$$\omega_x(t)=\sup\{r\in \mathbb{R}^+\,|\, t\in T(K)_r\}=\min\{v\big(\chi(t)-1\big)\,|\, \chi\in X^*(T)\}.$$
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, this $p$-valuation is saturated, and given by the Moy-Prasad filtration associated to the point $x\in \mathcal B(G)$ via
$$\omega_x(g)=\sup\{r>0\,|\, g\in G_{x,r}\}$$
for all $g\in G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is a generalization of \cite[Proposition 3.5]{LS}.  Uniqueness is clear, as any $p$-valuation compatible with the Iwahori factorization will be determined by its restriction on each factor, where its values are determines by properties (b) and (c).  

Existence is similarly easy: suppose first that $v\in X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$, and fix $(E,t)$ for $t=\mu(c)$ as in the proof of Lemma \ref{conjlemma}.  Then the $p$-valuation on $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ is defined by 
$$\omega_x(g)=\frac1{e_E}\cdot \sup\{n\in \mathbb{Z}^+\,|\, tgt^{-1} \in K_n\},$$
and we obtain properties (a), (b), (c), and (d) by comparing the Iwahori factorization of $I$ and the analogous factorization of $K_n$, exactly as in the proof of Lemma \ref{conjlemma}.  We can then allow the case where $v\in V(S_\mathrm{ad})$ does not lie in $X_*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$ by a simple application of Lemma \ref{limits}.  Indeed, use Lemma \ref{density} to construct a sequence of points $x_n\in \mathcal A(S)$ converging to $x$ which satisfy the requirements that $G_{x_n,\frac1{p-1}+}=G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ and $v_n\coloneqq x_n-x_0\in X*(S_\mathrm{ad})_\mathbb{Q}$ for every $n$.  Then the $p$-valuations $\omega_{x_n}$ converge pointwise to the function $\omega_x$, which is bounded away from $\frac1{p-1}$, proving that $\omega_x$ is a $p$-valuation by Lemma \ref{limits}.

To see that $\omega_x$ is also given by the characterization using the Moy-Prasad filtration, we note that by \cite[Proposition 13.2.5]{KP} there is for all $r>0$ an Iwahori factorization on $G_{x,r}$.  Specifically, the product map
$$\prod_{\alpha\in \Phi^{-,\mathrm{nd}}} U_{\alpha, x, r}\times T(K)_r\times \prod_{\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}} U_{\alpha, x, r}\to G_{x,r}$$
is a bijection.  It is now sufficient to show that the $p$-valuation $\omega_x$ agrees with the Moy-Prasad filtration on each Iwahori factor.  By construction, the two filtrations on the tori are equal, and the proof of Proposition \ref{root-group-pval} shows that the described filtrations on the root groups are precisely those coming from the Moy-Prasad filtration, as claimed.

Finally, as $\omega_x$ is compatible with the Iwahori factorization, it is enough to show that $\omega_x$ is saturated on each Iwahori factor to conclude that it is saturated on $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ by Remark \ref{compatible-saturation}.  Corollary \ref{torus-saturation} shows that $\omega_x$ is saturated on $T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$, and Proposition \ref{root-group-pval} shows that it is saturated on $U_{\alpha, x, \frac1{p-1}+}$ for each $\alpha\in \Phi^{\mathrm{nd}}$.

label: general-existence
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Fix any $x\in \mathcal B(G)$.
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont(1)]
\item $G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ is a $p$-torsion free pro-$p$ group.
\item For any $r>\frac1{p-1}$, $G_{x,r+1}=\{g^p\,|\, g\in G_{x,r}\}$.
\item \label{uniform} For any $r\geq 1$, $G_{x,r}$ is a uniform pro-$p$ group.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
These statements all are easy to prove for any finite rank saturated pro-$p$ group $(G,\omega)$, and are not unique to our situation.  Fact \ref{uniform} is perhaps the least standard, so we will prove that one for the convenience of the reader.  Because $p$-valued groups are always torsion-free, we know by \cite[Theorem 4.5]{DDMS} that it is sufficient to prove for any $r\geq 1$ that $G_r=\{g\in G\,|\, \omega(g)\geq r\}$ is powerful.  Indeed, given any $x,y\in G_r$, we have that
$$\omega([x,y])\geq \omega(x)+\omega(y)\geq 2r\geq r+1,$$
so the saturation yields some $z\in G_r$ such that $z^p=[x,y]$.  This means that $G_r/(G_r)^p$ is abelian, so $G_r$ is powerful, as desired.

label: torus-assumption
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{torus-assumption}
Using the Iwahori decomposition, we see that $G_{x,0+}=G_{x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ if and only if $T(K)_{0+}=T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$ and $U_{\alpha,x,0+}=U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{\mathrm{nd}}$.  If $T\cong \prod_{i=1}^m R_{L_i/K}\mathbb{G}_m$ is in fact an induced torus, then the condition that $T(K)_{0+}=T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$ translates exactly to the requirement that $p-1>e_{L_i}$ for all $i$, however for more general weakly induced tori it is difficult to reduce this assumption to a simpler statement.
head: environment

label: qpslit-zeroplus-roots
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{qpslit-zeroplus-roots}
For $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$, the condition $U_{\alpha,x,0+}=U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ holds if and only if 
$$\frac1{p-1}<\langle \alpha,v\rangle,$$
and $U_{-\alpha,x,0+}=U_{-\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ holds if and only if 
$$\langle \alpha,v\rangle<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix any $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$, and write $a\coloneqq \langle \alpha,v\rangle$ for convenience.  By \cite[Fact 6.4.5]{KP}, we have that $a\in \left(0,\frac1{m_\alpha e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}\right)$.

Our analysis will use similar ideas to those in the proof of Lemma \ref{density}.  Suppose that $\alpha$ is first of type R1, so as in Subsection \ref{R1} we have an isomorphism $u_\alpha:K_{\tilde\alpha}\xrightarrow{\sim} U_\alpha(K)$ which satisfies
$$U_{\alpha,x,r+}=\{u_\alpha(x)\,|\, v(x)+a>r\}=u_\alpha(\mathfrak m_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}^i)$$
for all $r\geq 0$, where $i$ is the least integer strictly greater than
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(r-a\right),$$
which can be described succinctly as 
$$i=1+\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(r-a\right)\rfloor.$$
We then see that $U_{\alpha,x,0+}=U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ if and only if 
$$\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}-a\right)\right\rfloor=\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}(-a)\rfloor,$$
and the latter is equal to $-1$.  It is easy to see that this condition is thus equivalent to $a>\frac1{p-1}$.  Similarly, $U_{-\alpha,x,0+}=U_{-\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ holds if and only if 
$$\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}+a\right)\right\rfloor=\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot a\rfloor,$$
and the latter automatically equaling 0 means this is equivalent to requiring
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot \left(\frac1{p-1}+a\right)<1.$$
This is precisely the same as saying $a<\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}$.

Suppose now that $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$ is of type R2, so now $0<a<\frac1{2e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}$.  Similar to the previous case, we have by Remark \ref{R2-desc} that $U_{\alpha,x,0+}=U_{\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ if and only if 
$$\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(\frac1{p-1}-a\right)\right\rfloor=\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}(-a)\rfloor\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(\frac1{p-1}-2a\right)\right\rfloor=\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}(-2a)\rfloor.$$
The latter values in both expressions equal $-1$, so this is equivalent to requiring
$$e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(\frac1{p-1}-a\right)<0\quad\mathrm{and}\quad e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(\frac1{p-1}-2a\right)<0;$$
the former is a stricter condition since $a>0$, and can be rewritten as $a>\frac1{p-1}$.  One also has $U_{-\alpha,x,0+}=U_{-\alpha,x,\frac1{p-1}+}$ if and only if 
$$\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(\frac1{p-1}+a\right)\right\rfloor=\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot a\rfloor\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\left\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot\left(\frac1{p-1}+2a\right)\right\rfloor=\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot 2a\rfloor;$$
in this case, the latter is a stricter condition, and $\lfloor e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}\cdot 2a\rfloor=0$ means that it can be rewritten as 
$$a<\frac12\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right).$$
head: environment

label: polytope
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{polytope}
If $G$ is quasisplit, $T$ is weakly induced, and $T(K)_{0+}=T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$, then there is an open convex polytope $U$ of the dominant base chamber $C\subseteq \mathcal A(S)$ given by
$$U=\left\{x\in \mathcal A(S)\,\Bigg|\, x=x_0+v, \quad \frac1{p-1}<\langle \alpha, v\rangle<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right)\quad \forall \alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}\right\}$$
such that each point $x\in U$ corresponds to a distinct saturated $p$-valuation $\omega_x$ on $I$, which is described by the Moy-Prasad filtration at the point $x$.  This subset $U$ is nonempty precisely when 
$$p-1>(m_\alpha \mathrm{ht}(\alpha)+1)\cdot e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
One can easily check that $U$ is an open convex polytope using the conditions defining $U$: for each $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$, we have a linear functional $V(S_\mathrm{ad})\to \mathbb{R}$ given by $v\mapsto \langle \alpha, v\rangle$.  The set 
$$U_0\coloneqq \left\{v\in V(S_\mathrm{ad})\,\Bigg|\, \frac1{p-1}<\langle \alpha, v\rangle<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right)\quad \forall \alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}\right\}$$
is thus the intersection of finitely many open half-spaces, and is bounded as the set of simple roots $\Delta\subseteq \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$ forms a basis of the dual space $V(S_\mathrm{ad})^*$.  Then $U=x_0+U_0$ is indeed a convex open polytope in $C$.  

The only claim which remains unproven is the characterization of when $U$ is nonempty.  Say $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\ldots, \alpha_s\}\subseteq \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$ is a labeling for our simple roots, and set $a_i\coloneqq \langle \alpha_i,v\rangle$; choosing our point $x=x_0+v$ for $v\in V(S_\mathrm{ad})$ is equivalent to selecting values $a_i\in \mathbb{R}$ for $i\leq s$.  For each $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$, write $\alpha=\sum_i c^\alpha_i\alpha_i$ for $c^\alpha_i\geq 0$ with $\mathrm{ht}(\alpha)=\sum_i c^\alpha_i$.  Now $x\in U$ if and only if
$$\frac1{p-1}<\sum_i c_i^\alpha a_i<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right)$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$.  If this set is nonempty, we claim that we can set all of the $a_i$ to be the same value.  Indeed, choosing $\alpha=\alpha_i$ for each $i$ shows that $a_i>\frac1{p-1}$ for each $i$, and the only remaining conditions required for our choice of $a_i$ to result in a point lying inside $U$ are upper bounds on nonnegative linear combinations of the $a_i$ (as $c^\alpha_i\geq 0$).  Thus, we may shrink our values of $a_i>\frac1{p-1}$ without forcing $x$ to exit the set $U$, proving that there is some $\varepsilon>0$ such that $a_i\coloneqq\frac1{p-1}+\varepsilon$ for all $i$ results in a valid point within $U$.  Set $a\coloneqq \frac1{p-1}+\varepsilon$.  Note that now $\langle \alpha,v\rangle=\sum_i c_i^\alpha a=\mathrm{ht}(\alpha) \cdot a$.

Thus, to characterize when $U$ is nonempty, it is sufficient to check when there is some value $a\in \mathbb{R}$ such that 
$$\frac1{p-1}<\mathrm{ht}(\alpha)\cdot a<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right)$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$, which evidently exists precisely when 
$$p-1>(m_\alpha \mathrm{ht}(\alpha)+1)\cdot e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$.
head: environment

label: splitcase
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{splitcase}
Suppose that $G$ is split and $p-1>e_K h$ for $h=1+\max\{\mathrm{ht}(\alpha)\,|\, \alpha\in \Phi\}$ the Coxeter number.  Under these assumptions, $T$ is certainly weakly induced, and our condition $T(K)_{0+}=T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$ is automatically satisfied by Remark \ref{torus-assumption}.  Moreover, $U$ is nonempty by our above characterization, and one can verify that the barycenter $x$ of $C$ is an element of $U$.  As observed by \cite{dottolehung} (warning: their convention uses $v(p)=e_K$), the $p$-valuation constructed in \cite[Proposition 3.5]{LS} on the pro-$p$ Iwahori subgroup $I=G_{x,0+}$ is precisely the $p$-valuation $\omega_x$ in our notation for $x$ the barycenter of $C$.  Thus, Theorem \ref{general-existence} contains \cite[Proposition 3.5]{LS} as a special case.
head: environment

label: simplyconn
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{simplyconn}
Recall that if $G$ is quasisplit, semisimple, and simply connected, then its maximal torus $T$ is induced; more concretely, it can be written as 
$$T\cong \prod_{\alpha\in \Delta} R_{K_{\tilde\alpha}/K}\mathbb{G}_m.$$
Here, the map $R_{K_{\tilde\alpha}/K}\mathbb{G}_m\to T_\mathrm{sc}$ is given by the product
$$\alpha^\vee\coloneqq \prod_{\sigma\in \Theta/\Theta_{\tilde\alpha}} \sigma\tilde\alpha,$$
where this notation is justified by the fact that the composition of this with the canonical map $\mathbb{G}_m\to R_{K_{\tilde\alpha}/K} \mathbb{G}_m$ has image lying in $S$, and is precisely $\alpha^\vee:\mathbb{G}_m\to S$.  Thus, if we assume that $p-1>(\mathrm{ht}(\tilde\alpha)+1)\cdot e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}$, when $G$ is quasisplit, semisimple, and simply connected, it is immediate that $T$ is induced with $T(K)_{0+}=T(K)_{\frac1{p-1}+}$.  

We can use this to better understand the non-simply connected case as follows.  For $G$ a semisimple $K$-group, let $G_\mathrm{sc}$ denote its simply connected cover, and let $T_\mathrm{sc}$ denote the maximal torus given by the preimage of $T$ under the map $G_\mathrm{sc}\to G$.  In this case, the apartment $\mathcal A(S)=\mathcal A(S_\mathrm{sc})$ is an affine space over $V(S)=V(S_\mathrm{sc})$, where $S_\mathrm{sc}$ denotes the maximal split torus of $G_\mathrm{sc}$ lying in the preimage of $S$.
head: environment

label: qsplit-ss
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{qsplit-ss}
Suppose that $G$ is a connected quasisplit semisimple $K$-group, and assume that 
$$p-1>\big(m_\alpha\mathrm{ht}(\alpha)+1\big)\cdot e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}$$
for all $\alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}$.  Then the maximal pro-$p$ subgroups of $T(K)$ and $T_\mathrm{sc}(K)$ are canonically isomorphic, and the roots and root groups of $G(K)$ and $G_\mathrm{sc}(K)$ are identified as always, allowing us to conclude that the pro-$p$ Iwahori subgroups $I_\mathrm{sc}\subseteq G_\mathrm{sc}(K)$ and $I\subseteq G(K)$ associated to the chamber $C$ are isomorphic.  

In particular, all of Corollary \ref{polytope} applies to such a group $G$: there is an open convex nonempty polytope $U$ of $C\subseteq \mathcal A(S)$ given by 
$$U=\left\{x\in \mathcal A(S)\,\Bigg|\, x=x_0+v, \quad \frac1{p-1}<\langle \alpha, v\rangle<\frac1{m_\alpha}\left(\frac1{e_{K_{\tilde\alpha}}}-\frac1{p-1}\right)\quad \forall \alpha\in \Phi^{+,\mathrm{nd}}\right\}$$
such that each point $x\in U$ corresponds to a distinct saturated $p$-valuation $\omega_x$ on $I$, which is described by the Moy-Prasad filtration at the point $x$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove this, we will use an argument from the beginning of the proof of \cite[Proposition 12.1]{totaro}, which was also used in the more recent proof of \cite[Lemma 5.4]{dottolehung}.

Let $Z$ be the kernel of the map $G_\mathrm{sc}\to G$, which is a finite subgroup of the center of $G_\mathrm{sc}$.  As stated in \cite{totaro}, any prime number $q$ which divides the order of the center of a simply connected semisimple group is at most the maximum of the Coxeter numbers of its simple factors in the algebraic closure.  In particular, this means that $q\leq \max_{\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi} \mathrm{ht}(\tilde\alpha)+1$.  Thus, by our hypotheses, $Z$ has order prime to $p$.

We now have an exact sequence
$$Z(K)\to  G_\mathrm{sc}(K)\to G(K)\to H^1(K,Z)$$
by using Galois cohomology, and what we just said shows that $Z(K)$ is a finite abelian group with order prime to $p$, that hence has no pro-$p$ subgroups.  It is a standard fact that $H^1(K,Z)$ is finite (e.g., see \cite[Theorem 6.16]{PR}); we claim that $Z$ having order prime-to-$p$ implies that this finite abelian group $H^1(K,Z)$ also has order prime-to-$p$.  Indeed, we know that $H^1(K,Z)=\varinjlim_{L/K\text{ finite}}H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(L/K), Z(L))$, and thus there is some finite $L/K$ for which $H^1(K,Z)=H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(L/K), Z(L))$ as the former is finite.  Now the fact that $Z(L)$ is finite with order prime-to-$p$ gives us immediately that there are no elements of order $p$ in $H^1(K,Z)$.  Thus, our exact sequence $Z(K)\to G_\mathrm{sc}(K)\to G(K)\to H^1(K,Z)$ has on its ends finite abelian groups of order prime-to-$p$.
                                                                                                                                      

To fix notation, choose $x$ to be a point lying within $U$, so $I=G_{x,0+}$ and $I_\mathrm{sc}=(G_\mathrm{sc})_{x,0+}$.  Because $G_\mathrm{sc}$ is simply connected, $G_\mathrm{sc}(K)^0=G_\mathrm{sc}(K)$ (using the notation of \cite[Definition 2.6.23]{KP}) by \cite[Proposition 11.5.4]{KP}, hence $I_\mathrm{sc}$ is a maximal pro-$p$ subgroup of $G_\mathrm{sc}(K)$ by \cite[Proposition 13.5.2]{KP}.  Because $Z(K)$ has no pro-$p$ subgroups, the map $I_\mathrm{sc}\to G(K)$ is injective, and has image a maximal pro-$p$ subgroup of $G(K)$ since $H^1(K,Z)$ has no pro-$p$ subgroups.  
                                                                                                                                                                                               
Thus, the natural isogeny $I_\mathrm{sc}\to I$ must be an isomorphism as the latter is a pro-$p$ subgroup of $G(K)$.

In order to justify that the induced $p$-valuations on $I$ are coming from the Moy-Prasad filtrations on $G$ and not just from those on $G_\mathrm{sc}$, we must show that the isogeny of tori $\phi:T_\mathrm{sc}\to T$ arising from $G_\mathrm{sc}\to G$ preserves the minimal congruent filtration on the respective tori, i.e., that $\phi(T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_r^\mathrm{mc})=T(K)_r^\mathrm{mc}$ for any $r>0$.  Since $T_\mathrm{sc}$ is an induced torus, we know by \cite[Corollary B.10.13]{KP} that $T_\mathrm{sc}(K)^\mathrm{mc}_r=T_\mathrm{sc}(K)^\mathrm{std}_r$ is just the standard filtration.  By the functoriality of the minimal congruent filtration (see \cite[Proposition B.10.10]{KP}), we know that
$$\phi(T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_r^\mathrm{std})=\phi(T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_r^\mathrm{mc})\subseteq T(K)_r^\mathrm{mc}.$$
Since the minimal congruent filtration is admissible by \cite[Corollary B.10.13]{KP}, we know that $T(K)_r^\mathrm{mc}\subseteq T(K)_r^\mathrm{std}$ holds by \cite[Lemma B.10.4]{KP}, so it is sufficient to note that $\phi(T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_r^\mathrm{std})\supseteq T(K)_r^\mathrm{std}$.  To see this claim, note that our isogeny $\phi:T_\mathrm{sc}\to T$ induces an injection $X^*(T)\hookrightarrow X^*(T_\mathrm{sc})$ with finite cokernel.  Moreover, because $Z=\ker\phi$ has order prime-to-$p$, we find that the cokernel of $X^*(T)\hookrightarrow X^*(T_\mathrm{sc})$ has order prime-to-$p$; to fix notation, let $n$ be this order.  Suppose that $t\in T(K)_{0+}$ is any element of $T(K)_r^\mathrm{std}$, so by definition $v(\chi(t)-1)\geq r$ for all $\chi\in X^*(T)$.  To simplify notation, we identify $t$ with its unique preimage in $T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_{0+}$.  Fix any $\chi_0\in X^*(T_\mathrm{sc})$, so $\chi_0^n$ lies in the image of $X^*(T)$.  By hypothesis, we know $v(\chi_0(t)^n-1)\geq r$.  Since $t\in T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_{0+}$, write $\chi_0(t)=1+\varpi_E^i u$ for some finite $E/K$ which splits $T_\mathrm{sc}$, where $u\in \mathcal O_E^\times$.  Now
$$v(\chi_0(t)^n-1)=v((1+\varpi_E^i u)^n-1)=v(n\varpi_E^iu)=v(\varpi_E^iu)=v(\chi_0(t)-1),$$
so we conclude that in fact $v(\chi_0(t)-1)\geq r$ for all $\chi_0\in X^*(T_\mathrm{sc})$, and hence $t$ lies in $\phi(T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_r^\mathrm{std})$.  This proves that $\phi(T_\mathrm{sc}(K)_r^\mathrm{mc})=T(K)_r^\mathrm{mc}$ for all $r>0$.

title: Remark
body_md:
We note that our results subsume part of \cite[Proposition 12.1]{totaro}.  To show this, we will briefly recall the setup from that proposition.  Let $G$ be a connected semisimple group over $K$.  Then $G$ becomes quasisplit after base changing to $G_E$ over a finite unramified extension $E/K$ by \cite{Steinberg}.  The universal covering of $G_E$ is a product of restrictions of scalars of absolutely simple quasisplit groups $H_L$ over various finite extensions $L/E$.  Suppose that $p-1>h(H_L)e_L$, where $h(H_L)$ is a generalized Coxeter number defined to be
$$h(H_L)\coloneqq\max_{\tilde\alpha\in \tilde\Phi_{H_L}^+}(\mathrm{ht}(\tilde\alpha)+1)\cdot [L_{\tilde\alpha}:L]$$
if $H_L$ has reduced relative root system, and is twice this value if $H_L$ has nonreduced relative root system.  The relevant result of Totaro is that it follows that every pro-$p$ subgroup of $G(K)$ admits a $p$-valuation.

Given the same setup as in \cite{totaro}, we note that Corollary \ref{qsplit-ss} constructs a $p$-valuation on the pro-$p$ Iwahori of $G$ which is moreover saturated. Indeed, by Remark \ref{gen_invariants}, it is sufficient to show that we get a $p$-valuation on a pro-$p$ Iwahori $I$ of $H_L$ for any simple factor $H_L$ that is saturated.  Fix such a simple factor $H_L$.  Indeed, we first note that in Totaro's proof, he mentions that the condition $p-1>h(H_L)e_L$ implies that the maximal torus $T$ of $H_L$ splits over a finite extension $\tilde K/K$ with $e_{\tilde K}<p-1$, which means our condition on the torus in all the results above is automatically satisfied.  Next, we note that if $\tilde\alpha$ is a root of $H_L$ of type R1, then $e_L\cdot [L_{\tilde\alpha}:L]\geq e_{L_{\tilde\alpha}}$ implies automatically that $p-1>(\mathrm{ht}(\tilde\alpha)+1)\cdot e_{L_{\tilde\alpha}}$.  If there is some $\tilde\alpha$ which lies over a root of type R2 in the relative root system, then by the definition of the generalized Coxeter number in Totaro, we find that
$$p-1>2(\mathrm{ht}(\tilde\alpha)+1)\cdot [L_{\tilde\alpha}:L]\cdot e_L>(2\mathrm{ht}(\tilde\alpha)+1)e_{L_{\tilde\alpha}},$$
which implies as claimed that we get a saturated $p$-valuation on $I$.

title: Construction
body_md:
We now seek to construct a natural map
$$\mathrm{Lie}(G(K))\to \mathrm{Lie}(G)(K)$$
which will ultimately be an isomorphism of Lie $K$-algebras.  While one could conclude using a shorter argument based on \cite[Theorem 10.23]{milneAG} that these are abstractly isomorphic, we want to have an actual map with which we can perform computations; later, we will be comparing $\mathcal O_K$-lattices within these two Lie algebras via the map we construct.

One can summarize our identifications above as
$$\mathrm{Lie}(G(K))\cong \mathrm{Der}_e(G(K),K)\leq \mathrm{Hom}_K(C^\mathrm{an}(G(K),K),K)$$
and
$$\mathrm{Lie}(G)(K)\cong \mathrm{Der}_\epsilon(A,K)\leq \mathrm{Hom}_K(A,K)$$
where $G(K)=\mathrm{Hom}_{K-\mathrm{alg}}(A,K)$.  Note that any element $a\in A$ is a polynomial function on $G(K)$ (merely by evaluation), and in particular is locally analytic; thus, we have a map
$$A\hookrightarrow C^\mathrm{an}(G(K),K)$$
which is an inclusion as $A$ is reduced.  (We will often identify $A$ with its image under this map.)  This induces a map 
$$\mathrm{Hom}_K(C^\mathrm{an}(G(K),K),K)\to \mathrm{Hom}_K(A,K).$$

title: Lemma
body_md:
This restricts to a map 
$$\Phi_G:\mathrm{Der}_e(G(K),K)\to \mathrm{Der}_\epsilon(A,K),$$
which is functorial in $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $e\in G(K)=\mathrm{Hom}_{K-\mathrm{alg}}(A,K)$ is precisely the augmentation map $\epsilon:A\to K$.  Thus, if we have an $e$-derivation $\Delta$, which means
$$\Delta(fg)=\Delta(f)g(e)+f(e)\Delta(g)$$
for $f,g\in C^\mathrm{an}(G(K),K)$, it follows immediately that for $a,b\in A$, 
$$\Delta(ab)=\Delta(a)\epsilon(b)+\epsilon(a)\Delta(b).$$
Thus, $\Delta$ restricts to an $\epsilon$-derivation of $A$.  Functoriality in $G$ is clear.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first seek to show this when $G=\mathrm{GL}_n$, i.e., that $\Phi_{\mathrm{GL}_n}$ is an isomorphism of Lie algebras over $K$.  Indeed, since $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)\subseteq M_{n\times n}(K)$ is an open subset, we have a natural identification
$$\mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{GL}_n(K))=T_e(M_{n\times n}(K))=M_{n\times n}(K);$$
the exercise on \cite[p. 101]{schneiderbook} shows that this identifies the Lie brackets on both sides, where the right side has the Lie bracket coming from its associative algebra structure.  Similarly, \cite[p. 188]{milneAG} shows that a derivation $D\in D_\epsilon(B,K)$ (for $B=K[x_{ij},\det(x_{ij})^{-1}]$ the ring of regular functions on $\mathrm{GL}_n$) corresponds bijectively to an element $(a_{ij})\in M_{n\times n}(K)$ by $a_{ij}\coloneqq D(x_{ij})$, and this $K$-linear isomorphism
$$\mathrm{Lie}(G)(K)\cong \mathrm{Der}_\epsilon(A,K)\cong M_{n\times n}(K)$$
identifies the Lie brackets on both sides.  We then claim that the diagram
                                                                                                                                                                                                         
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=tiny]
	{\mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{GL}_n(K))} && {\mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{GL}_n)(K)} \\
	& {M_{n\times n}(K)}
	\arrow["{\Phi_{\mathrm{GL}_n}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\sim", from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\sim", from=2-2, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
commutes, which would prove that $\Phi_{\mathrm{GL}_n}$ is an isomorphism of $K$-Lie algebras.  Indeed, say $\Delta\in \mathrm{Der}_e(\mathrm{GL}_n(K),K)$, so there exists a unique $M=(m_{ij})\in M_{n\times n}(K)$ such that $\Delta=\Delta_M$, i.e., $\Delta(f)=(d_ef)(M)$ for $f\in C^\mathrm{an}(G(K),K)$.  It is now sufficient to show for any $i,j$ that $\Delta(x_{ij})=m_{ij}$, since this would prove that $\Delta$ restricts to the derivation in $\mathrm{Der}_\epsilon(A,K)$ uniquely determined by $M$.  This follows from the definition on \cite[p. 57]{schneiderbook}: we have the chart
$$\iota: \mathrm{GL}_n(K)\hookrightarrow M_{n\times n}(K),$$
and $\Delta(x_{ij})=(d_e x_{ij})(M)$ is defined by
$$d_ex_{ij}:T_e(\mathrm{GL}_n(K))\xrightarrow{\Theta_\iota^{-1}} M_{n\times n}(K)\xrightarrow{D_{I_n}(x_{ij}\circ \iota^{-1})}K.$$
This exactly says that $(d_ex_{ij})(M)$ is given by $D_{I_n}(x_{ij}\circ \iota^{-1})(M)$, where $D_{I_n}(x_{ij}\circ \iota^{-1})$ is the derivative at $I_n$ of $x_{ij}\circ \iota^{-1}$, which is defined on an open neighborhood of $I_n\in M_{n\times n}(K)$.  But this extends to a linear map $x_{ij}:M_{n\times n}(K)\to K$ defined on the full vector space, hence is its own derivative; this shows that $D_{I_n}(x_{ij}\circ \iota^{-1})(M)=m_{ij}$, as desired.  Thus, $\Phi_{\mathrm{GL}_n}$ is an isomorphism of Lie $K$-algebras.

For our more general case, since $G$ is a linear algebraic group, we can pick an embedding $G\hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_n$, which induces an embedding $G(K)\hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$.  We then have a commutative diagram
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{GL}_n(K))} & {\mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{GL}_n)(K)} \\
	{\mathrm{Lie}(G(K))} & {\mathrm{Lie}(G)(K).}
	\arrow["{\Phi_{\mathrm{GL}_n}}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow["{\Phi_G}", from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-2, to=1-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
where we now know that the top arrow is an isomorphism; this immediately implies that $\Phi_G$ is injective.  This is now a $K$-linear injective map of $K$-vector spaces of equal dimension (both equal to $\dim_K(G(K))=\dim(G)$ by \cite[p. 101]{schneiderbook} and \cite[Proposition 1.37]{milneAG}), hence is a $K$-linear isomorphism.  But we know the vertical arrows preserve Lie brackets by naturality, and the top arrow preserves Lie brackets by our earlier argument, so we can conclude that $\Phi_G$ is an isomorphism of Lie $K$-algebras.

label: int-model-rem
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{int-model-rem}
Let $\mathcal G=\operatorname{Spec} B$ be an integral model of $G$ over $\mathcal O_K$, in the sense of \cite[Definition 2.10.1]{KP}, which we assume to be a linear algebraic group over $\mathcal O_K$ in a way compatible with the structure on $G$; thus, we may also use $\epsilon$ to denote the augmentation map $B\to \mathcal O_K$.  By \cite[Remark 2.10.8]{KP}, the Lie algebra 
$$\mathrm{Lie}(\mathcal G)(\mathcal O_K)\coloneqq \ker\left(\mathcal G(\mathcal O_K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon\mapsto 0} \mathcal G(\mathcal O_K)\right)$$
is canonically identified with $\mathrm{Der}_\epsilon(B,\mathcal O_K)$ via $\epsilon+\varepsilon D\mapsto D$, where $\mathrm{Der}_\epsilon(B,\mathcal O_K)$ is defined to be the $\epsilon$-derivations, i.e., the $\mathcal O_K$-linear maps $D$ satisfying 
$$D(ab)=D(a)\epsilon(b)+\epsilon(a)D(b)$$
for $a,b\in B$.  Then the same remark says that the canonical map $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathcal G)(\mathcal O_K)\hookrightarrow \mathrm{Lie}(G)(K)$ is injective with image an $\mathcal O_K$-lattice in this $K$-vector space.

We also note that \cite[Remark 2.10.3]{KP} says $\mathcal G(\mathcal O_K)$ is open in $G(K)$, hence $\mathcal G(\mathcal O_K)$ is also an analytic $K$-group.

\label{R1-LieAlg}
